items.label: f02-row-vs-total-drift
items.front: Legacy amount 0.005 stored with three decimals: how could the row and the ledger total disagree before normalizeAmounts?
items.back: The total counts Math.round(0.005 * 100) = 1 cent and the row displays $0.01 while storage keeps three decimals; one edit later the two disagree. Snapping to the cent at load keeps them consistent.

items.label: f04-unlabelled-total-scope
items.front: What defect does the existing budget dashboard have around its totals, per Exercise 2?
items.back: The totals are whole-ledger numbers that ignore the type filter and search, but the label does not say so. Put the scope in the label: All transactions or Matching the current filter.

items.label: f03-failed-delete-four-checks
items.front: A failed delete (setItem throws) must leave four things unchanged. Which four?
items.back: The in-memory array (length and the id), the stored string byte for byte, the editor (resetForm did not run), and #message reading Could not save rather than Transaction deleted.

items.label: f01-zero-record-pinned
items.front: Which test pins that a stored zero amount is readable but cannot be re-saved, and why pin a rough edge at all?
items.back: "a stored zero amount is readable but cannot be re-saved, by design": submit shows the positive-amount message, the record stays, and delete still works. Pinning makes changing the rule a decision, not an accident.

A value's validity would depend on how the user reached the form, a rule that later surprises whoever reuses the parser a third way
Passing an options object breaks the regex test at the top of parseCents
It would let users create brand-new zero transactions through the add form

choices.text: The browser would retry the write on the next render, so the data eventually persists
Nothing different: the catch block restores the previous array automatically
The screen would show the change, but it would vanish on reload because storage never received it
The old data would be lost from storage, because a failed setItem clears the key

choices.text: It lets the editor accept zero without touching parseCents
It avoids ever having to write a test for legacy data
It is the cheapest change, because loadTransactions already deletes invalid records
It keeps a single input rule and also makes the impossible state impossible inside the program

items.explanation: Position 3 keeps one rule for input and makes the impossible state impossible. The general lesson: ask what a tightened validator does to data that already exists.

items.prompt: To give field-specific money errors, why should parseCents return a reason (`{ error: "too-many-decimals" }`) rather than saveTransaction re-testing each condition?

choices.text: Returning a reason lets the parser show the message itself, removing setMessage
Handlers cannot run regular expressions on input events
Re-testing creates a second copy of the money rules that will drift from the parser; with a returned reason one place decides what money is and the handler only maps it to text
Re-testing in the handler would run the regex twice, which is too slow for large ledgers

choices: Returning a reason lets the parser show the message itself, removing setMessage

Re-testing in the handler would run the regex twice, which is too slow for large ledgers

items.explanation: Exercise 1: re-testing in saveTransaction gives a second copy of the rules and guarantees they will disagree within a month. One place decides what money is.

items.prompt: A refactor replaces parseCents with `Math.round(Number(text) * 100)` and keeps the `> 0` check. Which inputs now get through that the current parser rejects, and why?

choices.text: Only amounts above 999999999.99, because Number has no upper bound while the regex does
Text such as "1e3" or " 5 " becomes a valid amount, because Number accepts forms outside the plain-decimal grammar the parser enforces with its regex
Only negative values, because Math.round turns -0.4 into 0 which then passes as zero cents
None: Number rejects scientific notation and surrounding whitespace with NaN, so the two are equivalent

choices: Only amounts above 999999999.99, because Number has no upper bound while the regex does
Text such as "1e3" or " 5 " becomes a valid amount, because Number accepts forms outside the plain-decimal grammar the parser enforces with its regex
Only negative values, because Math.round turns -0.4 into 0 which then passes as zero cents
None: Number rejects scientific notation and surrounding whitespace with NaN, so the two are equivalent

items.explanation: 02-CONCEPTS: Number accepts forms that do not belong in this currency workflow; define the grammar before conversion. parseCents tests a plain-decimal regex first, then builds integer cents from the whole part and the padded fraction.

choices.text: Amounts with two decimals overflow safe integers; store amounts as strings instead
It rounds 0.105 to 10 cents; use Math.ceil before multiplying
It converts again on every later load ($12.50 becomes $1250.00 on the second run); store an envelope with schemaVersion and an explicit v1 to v2 function
Negative expenses flip sign; store income and expense in separate arrays

Negative expenses flip sign; store income and expense in separate arrays

items.explanation: Nothing records that the conversion already happened, so it double-converts silently for every user. A version marker makes the migration decidable.

items.prompt: normalizeAmounts snaps legacy amounts like 0.105 to the cent in memory on load but does not write them back. Why that choice?

choices.text: Writing on load would let a read fail a write, so a user with a full disk could not even open the budget; the snapped value is persisted by the next successful commit instead
localStorage cannot be written during page load, only after the first user event
The original values must be kept forever so the migration can be rolled back
Writing back would double-round the values on every reload

choices: Writing on load would let a read fail a write, so a user with a full disk could not even open the budget; the snapped value is persisted by the next successful commit instead
localStorage cannot be written during page load, only after the first user event
The original values must be kept forever so the migration can be rolled back
Writing back would double-round the values on every reload

items.explanation: The code comment: nothing is written back, so a read can never fail a write. Exercise 4 spells out the cost of the alternative: a user with a full disk cannot open their budget at all.
